title: All Work And No Play Makes Jack a Dull Boy: Understanding and Preventing Catastrophic Strategy Collapse in RLVR

paper.title: All Work And No Play Makes Jack a Dull Boy: Understanding and Preventing Catastrophic Strategy Collapse in RLVR
paper.abstract: Abstract During post-training of large language models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), GRPO-style algorithms can exhibit severe late-stage collapse. Prompt-based probing reveals that this is not benign strategic pruning, but a harmful contraction of effective strategy capacity that makes distinct reasoning strategies increasingly inaccessible. To characterize this phenomenon, we define strategies through trajectory-level policy-update interactions and develop a unified theoretical framework combining optimization dynamics and information theory. We prove that major RLVR objectives progressively concentrate probability mass onto a single strategy, while sustaining nontrivial task accuracy requires a minimum strategy capacity. The conflict between these two results provides a mechanistic explanation for catastrophic collapse. We further derive the Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI) as a lightweight online warning signal. To prevent collapse, we propose Mesh Learning , which exposes multiple reasoning strategies and prevents any single strategy from dominating optimization. Across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench, Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen and Phi model families, with gains of up to 13.4 pp and 11.5 pp, respectively. These results establish strategy preservation as a key principle for stable RLVR. Code is available at GitHub .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In recent years, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly in mathematics and coding ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Team et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Driven by verifiable outcome supervision and scalable critic-free policy optimization, RLVR has been rapidly adopted in both academia and industry, giving rise to a range of optimization frameworks, including GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , and GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , as well as regularization schemes based on KL divergence ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and JS divergence ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Together, these developments have established RLVR as a core post-training paradigm for modern reasoning models. Despite its effectiveness in improving reasoning performance, RLVR can exhibit severe late-stage instability. Prior studies have reported similar collapse behaviors ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and we observe the same phenomenon systematically in our experiments. As shown in Fig. 1 , accuracy drops abruptly after a period of seemingly successful optimization across two model families, Qwen ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Phi ( Abdin et al., 2025 ) , and five representative training recipes, including GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, GRPO+KL, and GRPO+JS. We call this abrupt degradation collapse . Its recurrence across prior studies, model families, algorithms, and regularization schemes suggests a shared limitation of current RLVR optimization, yet its underlying mechanism remains poorly understood. To characterize this behavior across RLVR algorithms, we develop a unified theory grounded in the optimization dynamics of policy updates. Since individual trajectories rarely recur exactly and are too fine-grained to describe reasoning behavior, we introduce strategies as groups of trajectories that evolve coherently under parameter updates, and derive their distribution updates from the underlying trajectory-level updates. Within this framework, we explain collapse by contradiction through two central theorems: 1) If RLVR objectives (GRPO, DAPO, GSPO) persist in a non-collapse regime, the optimization inherently drives the policy toward a single dominant strategy with high probability; 2) achieving nontrivial task accuracy requires the model to retain a minimum strategy capacity. Together, these results reveal a fundamental conflict: RLVR optimization progressively contracts strategy capacity, while successful reasoning requires sufficient capacity to remain available. This contradiction provides a mechanistic explanation for the catastrophic collapse observed in practice. This mechanistic view also suggests what to monitor before accuracy collapses: the latent concentration of strategy dynamics. Since this transition is difficult to observe from standard training signals, we derive the Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI) from the geometry of RLVR updates as a lightweight online proxy for strategy collapse, requiring no auxiliary training and little computational overhead. Calibrating MEI on pre-RLVR models yields a 3 ​ σ 3\sigma alarm threshold for detecting departure from the non-collapsed regime before the accuracy cliff. Across model families, RLVR algorithms, and regularization schemes, MEI rises above the threshold ahead of the eventual accuracy cliff, consistently tracking the theoretically predicted transition. Independent strategy-level analysis further confirms that this transition corresponds to the loss of distinct reasoning strategies, supporting strategy collapse as a shared mechanism underlying late-stage RLVR failure. Building on the theoretical characterization and online measurability of strategy collapse, we propose Mesh Learning , a strategy-preserving RLVR framework that prevents individual strategies from dominating optimization and preserves multiple viable reasoning strategies throughout training. It consists of two complementary components: 1) Coach Prompting (CP) , which augments each query with strategy prefixes that elicit distinct solution approaches and ensure broad strategy exposure; and 2) Strategy-Balancing Regularization , which balances the learning progress across strategies to prevent any single strategy from overwhelming the others. In this way, CP constructs a diverse strategy mesh, while the regularizer preserves it throughout optimization. Across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2023 ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , and LiveCodeBench (v6) ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong RLVR and divergence-regularized baselines across both Qwen and Phi families, with gains of up to 13.4 and 11.5 percentage points (pp), respectively. These results highlight strategy preservation as a key principle for stable and effective RLVR optimization. In summary, our contributions are as follows: ❶ We establish a unified theory of RLVR dynamics, showing that inherent competition drives strategy concentration and explaining collapse through its conflict with the minimum strategy capacity required for successful reasoning. The analysis also yields MEI as a lightweight online indicator. ❷ We propose Mesh Learning , combining Coach Prompting and Strategy-Balancing Regularization to expose diverse reasoning strategies and prevent any strategy from dominating optimization. ❸ We provide extensive empirical validation across RLVR recipes and model families on AIME25/26, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, and LiveCodeBench, confirming the predicted collapse dynamics and the effectiveness of Mesh Learning.

sections.heading: 2 From Trajectory to Strategy
sections.text: Since the exact recurrence of an individual trajectory is exceedingly unlikely, analyzing isolated trajectories provides limited insight into training dynamics. To study these dynamics more effectively, we introduce the notion of a strategy , which captures a group of trajectories that respond coherently to local policy updates, i.e., they tend to be reinforced or suppressed together.

sections.text: Def. 1 is deliberately optimizer-centric, grouping trajectories solely by their interactions under policy updates without semantic assumptions. We next investigate whether these strategies align with human-recognizable solution methods, enabling both interpretation and explicit control. Figure 2: Semantic interpretability of strategies. sections.heading: 3.4 Why Divergences Fail
4 Methodology: Mesh Learning
sections.text: Sec. 3 shows that preventing RLVR collapse requires preserving sufficient strategy capacity. This creates two challenges: training rollouts must elicit distinct strategies, and no single strategy should dominate optimization. We therefore propose Mesh Learning with two components: 1) Coach Prompting , which elicits multiple reasoning strategies for each query, and 2) Strategy-Balancing Regularization , which prevents any strategy from dominating optimization. Under the conditions analyzed in Appendix C.2 , we further prove that the resulting dynamics converge to equilibrium retaining nonzero probability mass for every strategy. The pipeline of Mesh Learning is shown in Fig. 5 , it replaces homogeneous GRPO rollouts with multi-strategy exploration and jointly optimizes GRPO with Strategy-Balancing Regularization. Figure 5: Mesh Learning versus standard GRPO. Mesh Learning elicits multiple strategies and balances their relative growth during optimization.

sections.heading: 4.1 Strategy Elicitation: Coach Prompting
sections.text: Figure 6: Coach Prompting. An offline Coach LLM generates fixed strategy prefixes for training; at inference, the policy proposes its own strategy and follows the same verification procedure. Sec. 2.2 empirically shows that trajectories using the same human-recognizable solution method exhibit similar coupling patterns, motivating solution-method prefixes as practical proxies for the latent strategies in Def. 1 . We therefore introduce Coach Prompting (CP) to expose multiple strategies for each training query. For each query Q Q , an offline Coach LLM generates m m semantically distinct strategy prefixes, each specifying a candidate method, optionally with a brief description, but excluding calculations, intermediate solutions, and final answers. Each prefix conditions a separate rollout group, ensuring explicit exploration of all m m strategies rather than relying on spontaneous policy discovery. These prefixes are generated once and fixed throughout training, incurring no online Coach cost. During training, each prefix is treated as a candidate rather than a fixed instruction: the policy assesses its applicability, underlying mechanism, and alternatives before answering. At inference, no pre-generated prefix is provided; the policy proposes a candidate strategy itself and follows the same verification procedure, requiring no Coach LLM at test time. Coach-provided tokens are masked from the training loss. Full prompts and implementation details are provided in Appendix D.1 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models and Data. We run full experiments on Qwen3-4B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with additional cross-family experiments on Phi-4-mini-reasoning. Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini-reasoning use thinking mode, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct uses standard instruction-tuned generation. For MATH-500, we train on the 7,500 7{,}500 -problem Hendrycks-MATH training split ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) ; for AIME25/26 and GPQA-Diamond, we use 7,000 7{,}000 DAPOMath ( Yu et al., 2025 ) and 4,500 4{,}500 WildSci ( Liu et al., 2026 ) problems, respectively; and for LiveCodeBench, we use 4,500 4{,}500 Skywork-OR1-RL-Data problems ( He et al., 2025 ) . For Coach Prompting, each query is augmented with m = 4 m=4 distinct strategy prefixes generated offline by DeepSeek-V4-Pro and fixed throughout training. Training Configuration. Mesh Learning is implemented on top of GRPO using VeRL ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) , with the clip ratio set to 0.2 0.2 . For DAPO and GSPO, we follow the clip ratio configurations recommended in their original papers, while keeping all other hyperparameters identical across baselines. We use 16 16 rollouts per query and set the Strategy-Balancing Regularization weight to μ = 10 − 5 \mu=10^{-5} . Remaining configurations and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D.2 . Evaluation and Baselines. We evaluate on AIME25/26, MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , and LiveCodeBench (v6) ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , covering mathematical, scientific, and code reasoning. We compare Mesh Learning with GRPO, DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and GRPO with KL or JS regularization ( Li et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.text: Ablation for Coach-Prompting Priors. Since Coach Prompting provides extra strategy information, we compare each RLVR baseline with a CP-only counterpart using the same prefixes but without Strategy-Balancing Regularization. As shown in Table 2 , CP alone brings little or no improvement, while full Mesh Learning consistently performs better. This indicates that the gains do not come from stronger strategy priors alone, but from preserving these strategies during optimization. Number of Strategies. As shown in Table 2 , increasing m m from 3 3 to 4 4 leads to only small differences overall, showing that Mesh Learning is not sensitive to modest changes in m m . However, we found that an overly small m m limits the number of strategies exposed during training and therefore restricts the strategy capacity that can be preserved. We use m = 4 m=4 by default.

sections.heading: 6 Related Work
sections.text: RLVR optimization. Following GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , substantial work has improved RLVR through better sampling, clipping, importance weighting, and optimization objectives, including DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , CISPO ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , SAPO ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , VAPO ( Yue et al., 2025 ) , REINFORCE++ ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , GMPO ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and FAPO ( Ding et al., 2026 ) . These methods primarily improve RLVR’s optimization behavior, whereas we focus on the mechanism underlying its late-stage collapse. Understanding and Preventing Collapse. Recent work has documented collapse during prolonged RLVR training. Liang et al. (2026) show that Pass@1 improvements can coincide with reduced generation diversity and degraded high- k k Pass@ k k , while Nguyen et al. (2025) attribute reasoning-boundary shrinkage to negative interference and winner-take-all dynamics. Yuan et al. (2026) link diversity collapse to continued optimization on already-saturated problems, and M-GRPO ( Bai et al., 2025 ) studies abrupt performance collapse under long-horizon training. A common remedy is to constrain policy drift with fixed-reference KL regularization ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , while alternative divergences such as forward KL and JS have been shown to better preserve solution diversity ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, we provide a strategy-level theoretical account: starting from trajectory-level update interactions, we derive RLVR’s tendency toward strategy concentration and a complementary lower bound on the strategy capacity required for nontrivial task performance. Their tension directly explains catastrophic collapse and motivates Mesh Learning.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This work characterizes, anticipates, and mitigates catastrophic collapse in RLVR. We develop a strategy-level theory showing that RLVR progressively concentrates strategy mass, while successful reasoning requires sufficient strategy capacity; their conflict results collapse. This analysis further yields MEI as a lightweight online warning signal. We propose Mesh Learning , combining Coach Prompting and Strategy-Balancing Regularization to expose and preserve diverse strategies during optimization. Experiments across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench consistently demonstrate its effectiveness across Qwen and Phi model families. In conclusion, All Work And No Play Makes Jack A Dull Boy . RLVR may trade away strategy diversity for continued gains in reward, eventually exhausting the capacity required for further meaningful optimization. Our results highlight strategy preservation as a key principle for stable and effective RLVR.

sections.text: Since the strategy-level evolution equations derived for GRPO, GSPO, and DAPO share the same dynamical structure as Equation ( ⋆ ) (\star) , the analysis developed in Sec. A2.3 applies uniformly to all three RLVR objectives. Moreover, as established above, strategy-level probability redistribution occurs on a faster timescale than the internal rearrangement of trajectories within each strategy. Consequently, the dominant training dynamics are governed by competition among strategies, while the within-strategy trajectory distribution evolves only comparatively slowly. This timescale separation allows the long-term behavior of the policy to be characterized directly at the strategy level. Under GRPO, GSPO, and DAPO, differences in strategy advantage are progressively amplified, causing probability mass to concentrate toward an increasingly dominant strategy. In particular, once one strategy acquires a relative advantage, the resulting positive feedback further increases its probability and suppresses competing strategies, eventually driving the policy toward strategy concentration. Therefore, all three objectives systematically amplify the model’s existing preference over strategies. The strategy that is most favorable under the current model state—i.e., the one with the highest effective evolutionary advantage—is preferentially reinforced and becomes increasingly dominant, providing the dynamical mechanism underlying strategy collapse.

sections.heading: Convergence with our Method:
sections.text: In the converged state: As the model undergoes further optimization, the two initially entangled rationales are completely decoupled and distinctly preserved across our 10 evaluation rollouts, exhibiting an empirical macro-policy distribution of 30% for Strategy I and 70% for Strategy II. Furthermore, each sub-policy has crystallized into a highly deterministic response template, where trajectories generated within the same strategy share a token-level semantic similarity exceeding 95%, limited only to minor choices of words. This localized rigidity alongside global balance strongly demonstrates that our proposed regularization framework strictly maintains the equilibrium of macroeconomic policy proportions without interfering with the model’s capacity to optimize the localized execution of each specific strategy.
